headline: Spain struck over rent: nearly half a wage for a flat.
summary: Spain held its first general strike in 14 years on Wednesday, called by the main unions over housing and the cost of living. A 50 square metre flat in Madrid rents for €1,170 a month against an average salary of €2,460. The trigger was the eviction of an 87-year-old from the flat she had lived in for 70 years. Spain votes on November 29.

cover_question.q: Why did so many people stop work?

cover_answer: To make a point about rent. It costs half a Madrid wage.
table_question: When is it fair to stop everything to make people listen?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In Spain on Wednesday, lots of grown-ups did not go to work, on purpose. Buses and trains were a mess and some roads were blocked. They wanted the people in charge to see that a home costs too much, nearly half of what a grown-up earns, like spending half your pocket money on one toy. It is a way of being heard, and the grown-ups are talking about it.
5-7.why: A strike as being heard. Pocket money makes the rent real.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, and a strike is nothing they can see, so the script shows it as grown-ups staying home on purpose and roads blocked. The rent becomes half their pocket money on one toy, a cost they can feel. The eviction and the arrests stay off. Expect 'will you stop going to work?' No, not today.

8-12.script: A small flat in Madrid rents for €1,170 a month and the average wage is €2,460: nearly half a paycheck on a home, when the rule of thumb says a third. So Spain's unions called the first general strike since 2012, everyone off work at once so the country has to notice, like a whole class refusing to line up.
8-12.why: A rule, a number that breaks it, then the class refusing to line up.
8-12.why_long: At 9 they are working out whether rules get applied fairly, so the script gives them a rule, a third of a wage for rent, and a number that breaks it, nearly half. The strike then has a reason, and a whole class refusing to line up is a mechanism they have seen work. Expect 'did it work?' Not yet. Unions say huge turnout, bosses say low.

13-17.script: Can a government cheer a strike against itself? Spain's did: Sánchez called an election after parliament rejected his housing plan, then praised the walkout. Second: a Madrid flat takes nearly half the average wage, and the business lobby says that is not employers' fault. Whose problem is rent?
13-17.why: A government backing a strike, with the vote 18 days out.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: a strike is a protest against those in power, and this time the powerful are cheering it on, 18 days before a vote. At 16 they test whether you argue the motive honestly, so the script hands them the opposition's charge. Expect 'is it fair to measure rent against pay?' Yes. It is the standard measure.

5-7.q: Why did the grown-ups stop working?
5-7.a: To get noticed. Homes cost too much there, so everyone stayed off work for one day until the people in charge listened.

8-12.q: Why did so many people stop work?
8-12.a: A strike: one day off work, all at once, so the government notices the rent.
Dozens were arrested, the interior ministry said. Most people just marched.

13-17.q: Is the government using this for the election?
13-17.a: The opposition says exactly that. Sánchez says questioning the right to strike is the nonsense.

13-17.q: Why is rent so high there?
13-17.a: Rising interest rates, and red tape that stops new building, Semafor says.
